Life from age 4 to 16

Sometimes I want to find out what happens without entering a competition about it. I'm not against having plans; I just want the plans to leave enough room for the things that make a normal Tuesday good.

  • family: Lives with parents and an older sister; they share cooking and often host relatives for game nights.
  • finances: Working-class household with stable rent and little accumulated savings; Owen’s part-time earnings are mostly his to save.
  • geography: El Paso, Texas, near a bus route and several public parks.
  • cultureLanguages: Chinese American father and Mexican American mother; English and Spanish are used daily, with Cantonese phrases from grandparents.
  • school: Public early-college high school; enjoys some dual-credit courses but finds its frequent future planning repetitive.
  • accessOpportunities: Public library, community chess, school labs, and regional college or technical programs offer practical routes.
  • Age 4–5

    Owen liked drawing floor plans for houses where every room had an implausible purpose, including a room just for turning around. Adults kept his drawings because his explanations were so much fun to hear.

  • Age 6–7

    His sister taught him chess, and he liked reconstructing games more than playing rapidly. He also spent afternoons kicking a ball against a wall, pleased by the different sounds different surfaces produced.

  • Age 8–9

    Helping prepare dumplings and tamales introduced him to repeated tasks with many acceptable variations. He became good at noticing when a batch needed more water, but disliked anyone turning family cooking into a competition.

  • Age 10–11

    During remote lessons he took photographs of shadows moving across the patio and compared them over several days. A teacher suggested a science fair, but Owen preferred keeping a casual notebook without making a presentation.

  • Age 12–13

    Early-college classes brought older classmates and more responsibility for deadlines. He struggled initially with asking professors questions, then found that writing a precise email was easier than waiting until confusion had become overwhelming.

  • Age 14–15

    He began cashier shifts at a neighborhood market and appreciated coworkers who taught small practical shortcuts. Chess remained social rather than competitive, and he started sketching small comics about customers without using recognizable identifying details.

  • Age 16

    Owen currently combines dual-credit study, market shifts, and family cooking. He is curious about many systems but resists having every observation turned into an application; he wants affordable education with room for ordinary pleasures and a schedule he can sustain.

Life now

  • enjoys: Slow chess analysis · Shadow photographs · Family cooking
  • avoids: Turning hobbies into contests · Premature future labels
  • activities: Dual-credit classes · Market work · Community chess
  • demonstratedSkills: Writes clear requests · Handles transactions · Notices gradual visual changes
  • unfamiliarActivities: Orchestra · Welding · Organized wilderness trips
  • motivations: Understanding everyday systems · Keeping learning enjoyable
  • ambitions: Wants affordable continued education · Imagines a modest home near good food, public spaces, and people he can see regularly.
  • struggles: Asking questions early · Pressure to turn curiosity into credentials
  • supports: Sister · Parents · Market coworkers · College liaison
  • practicalConstraints: Work hours · Limited savings · Bus travel

Still uncertain: Would a longer self-directed investigation appeal? · Does he dislike public presentation or the pressure attached to it?
